title: Humid air narrows the gap
hook: Same temperature, 40% or 80% humidity: how much weaker is the drying push?

knows: Everyday objects have sizes, positions and amounts
doesNotKnow: that at the same temperature, the more water vapour already in the air, the weaker the push for water to leave the cloth, so drying slows in humid air

misconception: Humid air hardly slows drying; warmth is what matters.
objective: At equal temperature, higher relative humidity means a smaller difference between a wet surface’s saturation vapour pressure and surrounding water vapour. This model shows the gap, not a drying clock.

claims.text: At the same temperature, humid air already holds close to all the water vapour it can, so it takes water from a wet surface more slowly. The push is how far the air is from full.
claims.source: OpenStax College Physics 2e §13.6, https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/13-6-humidity-evaporation-and-boiling (opened 2026-10-14). Evaporation is inhibited by humidity. The card's constant flux is an explicitly illustrative assumption, not a measured household drying rate. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Opened OpenStax §13.6 (m42219): 'Relative humidity is related to the partial pressure of water vapor in the air. At 100% humidity, the partial pressure is equal to the vapor pressure ... If the partial pressure is less than the vapor pressure, then evaporation will take place'; 'evaporation is inhibited by high humidity'. At fixed temperature the saturation vapour pressure is fixed and partial pressure = RH x saturation pressure, so the gap is p_sat(1 - RH) and shrinks as RH rises. 'Shows the gap, not a drying clock': engine case 'humidity' computes only value = 1 - RH/100, labelled 'Normalised gap', with no time output. Reset to unverified 2026-10-15 by demo-builder (r11 fix plan wave W2: new prediction line, stage and reveal; engine 2). Re-verify against the rebuilt stage.

claims.text: Surface temperature, airflow and fabric also matter; no room-control advice is implied.

recall.question: Two rooms are at the same temperature: one at 40% relative humidity, one at 80%. In the lesson's normalised model, how do their vapour-pressure gaps compare?
options: Equal, since both rooms are at the same temperature
Twice as large in the 40% room
Three times as large in the 40% room
recall.why: Normalised gap = 1 − RH/100: 0.6 at 40% and 0.2 at 80%, three times larger. A smaller gap means less drive for evaporation. This is not a drying clock.
